paragraphs.heading: A star that explodes
paragraphs.text: A supernova is a powerful, brilliant explosion of a star. At its peak it can shine about as brightly as an entire galaxy, then it fades over several weeks or months. The star that blew up is called the progenitor. Afterwards it either collapses into a neutron star or a black hole, or it is destroyed completely and leaves behind a diffuse nebula.

paragraphs.heading: Two ways to blow up
paragraphs.text: Theory points to two main triggers. In the first, a white dwarf heats up enough for runaway nuclear fusion to start, and this tears the whole star apart; it can get there by gathering material from a companion star or by merging with another star. In the second, the core of a massive star suddenly collapses once fusion can no longer make enough energy to hold off the star's own gravity. That must happen once the star begins fusing iron, but it can happen at an earlier stage.

paragraphs.heading: What the blast leaves behind
paragraphs.text: A supernova can fling out several solar masses of material at up to several percent of the speed of light. This drives a shock wave into the interstellar medium around it, sweeping up a growing shell of gas and dust that is seen as a supernova remnant. Supernovae are a major source of the elements from oxygen to rubidium in the interstellar medium, and of cosmic rays. Their shock waves can set off the birth of new stars, and they might also make gravitational waves.

paragraphs.heading: How often they happen
paragraphs.text: In our galaxy a supernova is expected about once every 61 years on average, yet the last one seen was Kepler's Supernova in 1604. Studies of remnants in the Milky Way and of supernovae in other galaxies put the rate at about 1.6 to 4.6 per century. Apart from telescope discoveries, fewer than 10 have been recorded in the last 2,000 years. There is some evidence that the youngest known one, G1.9+0.3, went off in the late 19th century without anyone noticing, perhaps because dust along the galaxy's disk dimmed it.

paragraphs.heading: In the historical record
paragraphs.text: The first widely recorded supernova, SN 1006, appeared in the constellation Lupus and observers in China, Japan, Iraq, Egypt and Europe wrote about it. Chinese astronomers recorded SN 1054, the explosion that made the Crab Nebula. Tycho Brahe watched SN 1572 and Johannes Kepler watched SN 1604, the latest Milky Way supernovae seen with the naked eye. In Europe these two were used to argue against the Aristotelian belief that the universe beyond the Moon and planets never changes.

paragraphs.heading: Telescopes and SN 1987A
paragraphs.text: Telescopes made it possible to find fainter and more distant supernovae, starting with SN 1885A in the Andromeda Galaxy. Several thousand are typically seen in distant galaxies every year. SN 1987A showed up in 1987 in the Large Magellanic Cloud, which is a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. It came from the explosion of a blue supergiant star, and observations of it included the only measurements of astronomical neutrinos other than those from the Sun.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name comes from
paragraphs.text: The word comes from the Latin nova, meaning new, because the explosion looks like a bright new star for a while. The prefix super- separates these from ordinary novae, which are far dimmer. Walter Baade and Fritz Zwicky began using the word in astrophysics lectures in 1931.
